turn_text: They call him the Trump of South America. He said that they're trying to sell more stuff to China, but they're not going to sell Brazil to China. He's not out encouraging a lot of Chinese investment. And that's one thing that I was concerned about because when I was down there 10 years ago, they were talking about Chinese investing $20 billion so they could build new roads, new infrastructure. This new president is talking about $17 billion for infrastructure. And the way he says he's going to come up with it is through private financing. But he said he wasn't going to exclude China completely, but he wasn't going to really expect them to put much into it. So how realistic that is, I'm not sure. They built one road to the north, up to a river, and then the private sector built port and bought barges and so forth. They have another road that they're trying to finish, but they've still got 60 kilometers and haven't been paved. And it costs us about $60 a ton to export soybeans and it costs them $125 a ton. So we're still seeing a significant advantage in terms of transportation. And the other thing I learned in Brazil is that we need that differential because when I was down there before, they were double cropping in Madagascar so that they were double cropping corn and they were only getting about 75% yield on that second crop corn after soybeans. Now they are double cropping more cotton than they are corn because of it. new yields, varieties, technology, and so forth. And they're getting four to five bale per acre cotton on a second crop. And they're getting 60 to 70 bushels soybeans. They've increased their corn yields when they're using corn as a second crop to 160, 170 bushels that eat an acre compared to 75 to four. So you can see that if you got, you know, people in the U.S. tell them they're going to have a 70 bushel soybean crop and a 5-bale cotton crop and they would think they're going to have it.
